<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Rashida Tlaib, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia, Rep. Nikema Williams>: H.R. 6553 would reduce the safeguards for some of the largest banks, including guardrails that could have prevented three of the largest bank failures in U.S. history in 2023 when Silicon Valley Bank and other regional banks failed. Specifically, the bill increases the minimum threshold when mandatory so-called ``enhanced prudential standards'' (EPS) apply to a large bank, going from $250 billion to $370 billion in total assets. It also increases the minimum threshold for when regulators are able to apply any EPS to large banks, going from $100 billion to $150 billion in total assets. The bill also indexes these thresholds, and related regulatory thresholds,\1\ to rapidly grow based on an untested nominal Gross Domestic Product (``GDP'') metric that Trump's FDIC recently rejected, instead of using a more common inflation-based metric.
\1\ The Fed has established four categories of banks subject to EPS as follows, with more stringent requirements increasingly applied to the highest categories. Category I: U.S. G-SIBs, Category II: BHCs with more than $700 billion in total assets or $75 billion in cross-jurisdictional activity; Category III: all BHCs with more than $250 billion and other BHCs between $100 billion and $250 billion that pose greater risks compared to others; and Category IV: all other BHCs between $100 billion and $250 billion. For more information, see Fed, Federal Reserve Board finalizes rules that tailor its regulations for domestic and foreign banks to more closely match their risk profiles (Oct. 10, 2019).
After the 2008 global financial crisis, Congress enacted the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (``Dodd-Frank'') into law. One of the key reforms in the Dodd- Frank Act was a requirement that bank holding companies with more than $50 billion in total assets be subject to EPS.\2\ This meant they were subject to more stringent capital, liquidity, leverage, stress testing, resolution planning, and other requirements to ensure they were safe and sound as a means of promoting financial stability. In 2015, Congress considered a measure to relax this requirement for banks with less than $250 billion in total assets. Greg Becker, CEO of SVB, submitted a statement for the record urging support for this effort, arguing that his bank had a ``low risk profile'' and a ``traditional banking business model.''\3\ In 2018, Congress ultimately enacted reforms into law,\4\ when SVB had $53 billion in total assets before rapidly growing to have more than $200 billion in total assets. In 2019, Trump's regulators issued rules implementing the 2018 law and further relaxed requirements for or otherwise exempted bank holding companies with less than $250 billion from enhanced prudential standards.\5\
\2\ See CRS, Enhanced Prudential Regulation of Large Banks (May 6, 2019).
\3\ See Senate Banking Committee hearings, ``Examining the Regulatory Regime for Regional Banks,'' March 19 and March 24, 2015.
\4\ P.L. 115-174, S. 2155 (115th Congress), the Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act (EGRRCPA).
\5\ See Fed, Federal Reserve Board finalizes rules that tailor its regulations for domestic and foreign banks to more closely match their risk profiles (Oct. 10, 2019). Also see Davis Polk, The Final Tailoring Rules for U.S. Banking Organizations (Nov. 21, 2019), and Todd Phillips, How 2018 Regulatory Rollbacks Set the Stage for the Silicon Valley Bank Collapse, and How to Change Course, Roosevelt Institute (Mar. 15, 2023).
These deregulatory actions in Trump's first term likely contributed to the 2023 regional bank failures.\6\ For example, instead of being subject to robust semiannual, company-run stress tests and annual supervisory stress tests, SVB was scheduled to be subject to a supervisory stress test every two years. But given the timing of its rapid growth, the bank was not scheduled to receive its first supervisory stress test until 2024. Additionally, SVB was exempt from the liquidity coverage ratio (``LCR'') and only had to do quarterly internal liquidity stress tests. SVB was also exempt from Dodd-Frank's resolution planning requirements (referred to as ``living wills'') while only having to do a more narrow resolution plan separately required by the FDIC for insured depository institutions.\7\ Moreover, regulators allowed banks of SVB size to opt-out of capital requirements relating to accumulated other comprehensive income (``AOCI''), which allowed SVB to seem better capitalized than it was with a large amount of unrealized losses in their securities portfolio.\8\ The Fed estimated this AOCI opt out inflated SVB's capital ratio by nearly 2%.
\6\ For a comparison of what prudential requirements applied to Silicon Valley Bank before and after the deregulatory measures were implemented, see Table 12 of Fed, Review of the Federal Reserve's Supervision and Regulation of Silicon Valley Bank (Apr. 28, 2023).
\7\ SVB submitted their first and only IDI resolution plan in December 2022. See SVB, 2022 Covered Insured Depository Institution Resolution Plan: Public Section (Dec. 2022).
\8\ See Seeking Alpha, SVB Financial: Incompetence Allowed By Flawed Regulations (Mar. 12, 2023). For more info on enhanced prudential standards that applied to SVB, see pp 11-12 from their Form 10-K for the fiscal year ending Dec. 31, 2022.
Additionally, concerns have been raised with how Trump's regulators rolled back the Volcker Rule, which generally prohibits banking entities from engaging in proprietary trading or investing in or sponsoring hedge funds or private equity funds, may have contributed to SVB's failure.\9\ For example, one change finalized in 2019 allowed banks to realize short term profits from sales in their available for sale (``AFS'') securities portfolio, whereas this was previously prohibited by the Volcker Rule. In 2022, SVB reduced more than $15 billion in hedges on its AFS portfolio to only $563 million by the end of the year, leaving it more vulnerable to failure as the Fed continued to raise interest rates.
\9\ Better Markets, Federal Reserve Deregulation Caused the Failure of Silicon Valley Bank and the 2023 Banking Crisis (Mar. 27, 2023). Also see Better Markets, Ten Actions Necessary to Prevent Large Bank Failures, Strengthen the Financial System, and Protect Main Street Families (May 9, 2023); Better Markets, Banking Crisis Exemplifies the Fed's Enforcement Failures: Here's What to Do About It (May 15, 2023); and Better Markets Silicon Valley Bank Failure: Accountability and Path Forward (accessed May 15, 2023).
With respect to Signature Bank, it had $44 billion in total assets in 2018 before quickly growing to have more than $110 billion in total assets.\10\ First Republic Bank had $99 billion in total assets in 2018 before rapidly expanding to have more than $212 billion in total assets at the end of 2022. While rare among large banks, both of these banks did not have a bank holding company. While that meant that some of Dodd- Frank's original enhanced prudential standards would not have automatically applied,\11\ certain stress testing requirements would have applied prior to the 2018 law,\12\ and regulators used other authorities to apply other enhanced measures, such as resolution planning.\13\
\10\ See Fed, Large Commercial Banks--Statistical Release (Mar. 30, 2018).
\11\ Given how nonbank financial company is defined in the law, FSOC has authority to designate and subject any bank that does not have a bank holding company to enhanced prudential standards, though they have not done so to date.
\12\ Under the original Dodd-Frank provisions, Signature Bank and First Republic Bank would have been required to conduct annual company-run stress tests, and the bank could have been subject to annual supervisory stress tests at the Fed's discretion.
\13\ Signature Bank was required to submit a resolution plan for insured depository institutions (IDI) to the FDIC once every three years, though given the timing of when the crossed the $100 billion threshold, they had not done so before they failed. For more on IDI resolution plans, see FDIC, FDIC and Financial Regulatory Reform--Title I and IDI Resolution Plans (Jan. 3, 2023). For more info on enhanced prudential standards that applied to Signature Bank, see pp 22-37 from their Form 10-K for the fiscal year ending Dec. 31, 2022.
In addition to these regulatory rollbacks and gaps, the Fed's supervisory practices eased during Trump's first term with a shift in culture and expectations from Fed leadership. In investigating what contributed to SVB's failure, the Fed found that, ``In the interviews for this report, [Fed] staff repeatedly mentioned changes in expectations and pressure to reduce burden on firms, meet a higher burden of proof for a supervisory conclusion, and demonstrate due process when considering supervisory actions . . . . As a result, staff approached supervisory messages, particularly supervisory findings and enforcement actions, with a need to accumulate more evidence than in the past, which contributed to delays and in some cases led staff not to take action.''\14\ In a press conference, Fed Chair Powell said, ``I fully recognize that we made mistakes,'' agreeing that the Fed's supervisory and regulatory shortcomings contributed to SVB's failure.\15\
\14\ Fed, Federal Reserve Board announces the results from the review of the supervision and regulation of Silicon Valley Bank, led by Vice Chair for Supervision Barr (Apr. 28, 2023).
\15\ American Banker, Powell: Fed made `mistakes' in regulation and supervision on his watch (May 3, 2023).
Even though regulators were forced to use systemic risk tools to resolve SVB ($212 billion) and Signature Bank ($110 billion), H.R. 6553 would severely limit if not eliminate the application of EPS to similarly-sized banks. However, there does not appear to be much study with data and analysis to justify such changes proposed by the bill, and the bill provides no flexibility for regulators to make refinements that promote safety and soundness. Arguably, this bill is the opposite of what is a tiered and tailored approach to regulating regional banks: it uses arbitrary thresholds to either exempt or severely limit the application of risk-based prudential safeguards. At a minimum, it would be prudent to proceed with greater caution with respect to safeguards relating to the largest banks given the risk to financial stability even a $100 billion or $200 billion bank poses, as the 2023 regional bank failures demonstrated.
Furthermore, proponents of indexing thresholds with nominal GDP argue that using nominal GDP will capture both inflation and economic growth, and ensure these thresholds evolve over time to make the application of various regulatory criteria more dynamic.\16\ That said, nominal GDP does not capture industry growth (which may differ from economic growth), institution complexity, consumer impacts, or other factors that may be relevant in setting a threshold to include or exclude different entities from the application of certain obligations.
\16\ See Bank Policy Institute (BPI), Adjusting Regulatory Thresholds for Economic Growth (Sep. 9, 2024); BPI, The Economy Evolves Over Time--So Should Bank Regulations (Sep. 26, 2025).
Moreover, using nominal GDP will lead to more rapid increases to thresholds compared to inflation, exempting institutions that Congress may not have intended to exempt when it first enacted the law. Over the last ten years, nominal GDP grew by nearly 70% compared to a modest 37% increase based on CPI-W.\17\ Over the past three decades, nominal GDP increased by 299% compared to a 111% increase in CPI W.\18\ While lobbyists for large banks have advocated for the use of a nominal GDP growth,\19\ other stakeholders have suggested Congress consider inflation- based metrics or even more nuanced thresholds that are not based solely on asset size.\20\
